items.title: OpenAI shares ten major advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science achieved by its AI model Astra, including disproving longstanding conjectures and improving bounds in multiple fields [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science
items.summary:
OpenAI announced that its internal AI model Astra has made significant progress on ten longstanding open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, spanning areas such as high-dimensional geometry, coding theory, group theory, quantum complexity, and lattice cryptography. These results include disproving the Erdős unit-distance conjecture and Connes’s rigidity conjecture, establishing the existence of non-sofic groups, and providing new bounds on sphere packing and arithmetic circuit complexity.

The AI-generated proofs were formalized and verified using the Lean proof assistant, with human researchers preparing the manuscripts. OpenAI emphasizes its commitment to transparency and responsibility, acknowledging the collaborative role of AI and humans in producing these results and encouraging the mathematical community to engage with and build upon these findings. The initiative also includes providing free access to advanced AI tools for academic researchers to accelerate discovery.

items.title: Developer advocates manually retyping LLM-generated code to prevent cognitive debt and maintain understanding in personal projects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Prevent cognitive debt by manually retyping LLM-generated code
items.summary:
A developer describes a workflow where they manually type out code generated by large language models (LLMs) instead of directly copying it, aiming to maintain a deep understanding of their projects and avoid accumulating cognitive debt. They instruct their coding assistant to show proposed edits and commands in chat rather than automatically applying them, allowing for careful review and comprehension.

This approach slows down development compared to fully automated code generation but helps the developer build a mental model of the codebase, detect errors or hallucinations, and adapt the code to their preferences. The developer compares this method to traditional learning advice of typing out code examples to better understand them and plans to continue this practice to balance productivity with comprehension.

items.title: AirLLM enables 70B parameter LLM inference on a single 4GB GPU without quantization or pruning [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AirLLM 70B inference with single 4GB GPU
items.summary:
AirLLM is an open-source project that significantly reduces memory usage during inference, allowing large language models with up to 70 billion parameters to run on a single 4GB GPU. It achieves this without relying on quantization, distillation, or pruning techniques, and supports even larger models like Llama 3.1 405B on 8GB and DeepSeek-V3 671B on about 12GB by streaming sparse MoE model experts one at a time.

The project includes features such as model compression for up to 3x inference speed improvements, support for various popular models including Qwen, Llama 3.x/4, and DeepSeek versions, and compatibility with MacOS. AirLLM also offers tools for automatic model detection and loading, and supports CPU inference and non-sharded models, making it accessible for a wide range of hardware configurations.

items.title: Researchers introduce Counterfactual-Faithful Quantization to improve algorithmic recourse stability in quantized models, reducing recourse failures and intervention costs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Bits Break Recourse: Counterfactual-Faithful Quantization
items.summary:
Model quantization reduces memory and latency but can disrupt algorithmic recourse by invalidating small actionable changes that flip decisions in full-precision models. This study proposes counterfactual sensitivity metrics—Validity Drop and Counterfactual Recourse Gap—to measure how quantization affects recourse behavior and introduces Counterfactual-Faithful Quantization (CFQ), a training method that preserves recourse outcomes while optimizing quantizer parameters and bit allocation.

CFQ is compatible with standard quantizers and can be applied as a training-free calibration for post-training quantization. Experiments on datasets including Adult, German Credit, and COMPAS demonstrate that while standard quantization methods maintain accuracy, they degrade recourse stability; CFQ consistently reduces recourse failures and cost increases at matched accuracy and bit budgets, improving recourse reliability in compressed models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.17160v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model quantization is widely used to reduce memory, latency, and deployment cost, and is typically judged by whether predictive accuracy is preserved. In decision systems that provide algorithmic recourse, however, accuracy preservation is not sufficient: a small actionable change that flips the decision of a full-precision model may fail after quantization, or require a substantially larger intervention. This paper studies this deployment mismatch and introduces counterfactual sensitivity under quantization, a framework for measuring how compression changes recourse behavior. We propose two metrics: Validity Drop (VD), which measures the fraction of full-precision recourse actions that no longer achieve the target outcome after quantization, and Counterfactual Recourse Gap (CRG), which measures the increase in minimal recourse cost under the quantized model. To mitigate this failure mode, we introduce Counterfactual-Faithful Quantization (CFQ), a quantization-aware training method that jointly learns quantizer parameters and mixed-precision bit allocation while preserving the target prediction at teacher-generated recourse points. CFQ is compatible with standard LSQ/PACT-style quantizers and mixed-precision policies, and can also be instantiated as a training-free calibration procedure for post-training quantization. Experiments on Adult, German Credit, and COMPAS show that standard QAT and mixed-precision baselines can preserve accuracy while substantially degrading recourse stability. At matched accuracy and bit budget, CFQ consistently reduces VD and CRG; for example, on Adult, CFQ reduces VD/CRG from $0.121/0.162$ for an accuracy-centric mixed-precision baseline to $0.061/0.071$.

items.title: DRIFT framework improves large language model self-improvement with difficulty routing and rhythm gating, achieving new state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DRIFT: Difficulty Routing Self-DIstillation with Rhythm-Gated Exploration and Success BuFfer Training
items.summary: Researchers propose DRIFT, an online self-evolution policy optimization framework for large language models that dynamically adjusts training signals based on problem difficulty and focuses exploration on critical reasoning tokens. DRIFT incorporates a success buffer and a two-stage curriculum learning strategy to preserve high-quality experience and guide stable policy evolution. Evaluated on five benchmarks and three model scales, DRIFT outperforms previous methods GRPO and SDPO, achieving an average score of 79.5% and setting new state-of-the-art accuracy of 79.2% on the ToolUse benchmark.
items.description: Researchers propose DRIFT, an online self-evolution policy optimization framework for large language models that dynamically adjusts training signals based on problem difficulty and focuses exploration on critical reasoning tokens. DRIFT incorporates a success buffer and a two-stage curriculum learning strategy to preserve high-quality experience and guide stable policy evolution. Evaluated on five benchmarks and three model scales, DRIFT outperforms previous methods GRPO and SDPO, achieving an average score of 79.5% and setting new state-of-the-art accuracy of 79.2% on the ToolUse benchmark.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30345v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Enabling large language models to achieve stable self-improvement without external expert supervision remains a central challenge in complex reasoning tasks. Existing self-distillation and reinforcement learning methods lack explicit mechanisms for tracking problem-level learning progress and adapting optimization strategies accordingly. Consequently, training may over-optimize easy problems, receive weak supervision from hard problems, and fail to sufficiently explore borderline cases. To resolve these issues, we propose DRIFT, an online self-evolution policy optimization framework for large language models. DRIFT regulates the model's self-improvement process through the joint use of Difficulty Routing and Rhythm Gating. The former identifies the model's learning state at the problem level and dynamically allocates self-distillation and reinforcement learning signals, while the latter refines policy updates at the token level, concentrating exploration on critical reasoning positions. By further incorporating a success buffer and a two-stage curriculum learning strategy, DRIFT preserves high-quality historical experience while progressively guiding the model from reliable behavior acquisition toward stable policy evolution. Evaluated across five benchmarks and three model scales, DRIFT surpasses the peak performance of both GRPO and SDPO across all evaluated metrics. On the average score over the five benchmarks, DRIFT achieves 79.5$\%$, outperforming GRPO by 9.5$\%$ and SDPO by 7.5$\%$, establishing a new state-of-the-art result. Notably, on ToolUse, DRIFT reaches an accuracy of 79.2$\%$, improving over GRPO by 13.5$\%$ and SDPO by 10.7$\%$, setting a new state-of-the-art and substantially outperforming all concurrent methods.

items.title: Researchers propose ECHO, a selective turn-memory framework for traceable context reconstruction in agentic reinforcement learning, improving accuracy and efficiency on BrowseComp-Plus [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ECHO: Prune To Act, Trace To Learn With Selective Turn Memory In Agentic RL
items.summary:
Researchers introduce ECHO, a framework designed to improve long-horizon language agents' decision-making by selectively compressing and reconstructing past interactions with source-indexed memory records. This approach addresses the challenge of assigning credit to relevant evidence in bounded context windows during reinforcement learning.

ECHO outperforms previous methods like GRPO and SUPO on the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, achieving 43.4% held-out accuracy while using fewer turns and less trajectory data. The trained policy also demonstrates improved zero-shot generalization across various tasks, including multi-objective question answering, code generation, and information-seeking benchmarks on both dense and mixture-of-experts backbones.
items.description:
Researchers introduce ECHO, a framework designed to improve long-horizon language agents' decision-making by selectively compressing and reconstructing past interactions with source-indexed memory records. This approach addresses the challenge of assigning credit to relevant evidence in bounded context windows during reinforcement learning.

ECHO outperforms previous methods like GRPO and SUPO on the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, achieving 43.4% held-out accuracy while using fewer turns and less trajectory data. The trained policy also demonstrates improved zero-shot generalization across various tasks, including multi-objective question answering, code generation, and information-seeking benchmarks on both dense and mixture-of-experts backbones.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31650v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon language agents must repeatedly interact with tools, accumulate evidence, and make decisions under bounded context windows. Context-management methods make such rollouts feasible by simplifying past interactions through deletion, folding, or memory editing. However, when useful history is collapsed into compressed states, the reconstructed context may no longer reveal which earlier observations support a successful final answer. This creates a mismatch between bounded-context acting and outcome-based reinforcement learning: the policy acts on reconstructed context, while the learner lacks source-level provenance for assigning credit to the evidence that mattered. We propose ECHO, a selective turn-memory framework for traceable context reconstruction in Agentic RL. ECHO compresses each completed environment turn into a compact source-indexed memory record, reconstructs bounded policy contexts by selecting useful records, and reuses the selected source indices to route positive outcome credit to the final trajectory segment, reused evidence turns, memory findings, and memory-selection actions. On BrowseComp-Plus, ECHO reaches 43.4% held-out accuracy, outperforming GRPO at 28.9% and the rolling-summary baseline SUPO at 36.1%, while using fewer turns and lower trajectory volume than SUPO. The trained policy also improves zero-shot generalization across multi-objective QA, code generation, and deep information-seeking benchmarks on both dense and MoE backbones.

items.title: Researchers find cheap open-weight models can reliably judge natural-language mathematical proofs at up to 100 times lower cost than frontier LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cost-Effective Automated Judging of Natural-Language Mathematical Proofs
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated whether inexpensive open-weight models can effectively grade natural-language mathematical proofs compared to expensive large language model (LLM) judges. On a 200-instance validation set from IMO-GradingBench, three low-cost models—GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-V4 Flash, and Gemma-4 31B—matched human pass/fail decisions at rates statistically indistinguishable from leading models Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, while costing up to 100 times less. Extending the evaluation to the full 1000-instance benchmark, they found that requiring unanimous agreement among the three cheap judges yielded the highest precision and consistency across multiple runs.

The study suggests that these affordable models can serve as competitive automated judges for mathematical proofs, significantly reducing evaluation costs. The recommended consensus rule, requiring all three judges to pass a proof, was identified post-hoc and the authors note it requires independent replication before widespread adoption.
items.description:
Researchers evaluated whether inexpensive open-weight models can effectively grade natural-language mathematical proofs compared to expensive large language model (LLM) judges. On a 200-instance validation set from IMO-GradingBench, three low-cost models—GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-V4 Flash, and Gemma-4 31B—matched human pass/fail decisions at rates statistically indistinguishable from leading models Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, while costing up to 100 times less. Extending the evaluation to the full 1000-instance benchmark, they found that requiring unanimous agreement among the three cheap judges yielded the highest precision and consistency across multiple runs.

The study suggests that these affordable models can serve as competitive automated judges for mathematical proofs, significantly reducing evaluation costs. The recommended consensus rule, requiring all three judges to pass a proof, was identified post-hoc and the authors note it requires independent replication before widespread adoption.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grading natural-language mathematical proofs is a recurring cost in evaluating math-reasoning systems, and frontier LLM judges are expensive. We ask whether cheap open-weight models can serve as reliable judges given a candidate proof, a ground-truth proof, and a human-grading rubric. On a 200-instance validation sample of IMO-GradingBench, three cheap judges (GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-V4 Flash, Gemma-4 31B) agree with human pass/fail decisions at rates statistically indistinguishable from Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, at up to $100\times$ lower cost. We had expected a majority vote of the three to be the best budget option; it matched the frontier but did not improve on its strongest member. Extending to the full 1000-instance benchmark and exploring consensus rules, we found that requiring unanimous agreement (all-three-pass) reaches the highest pass-agreement and precision and, on four replicate runs, the smallest run-to-run spread. The headline finding is that cheap judges are competitive with the frontier at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost; as a deployable default we recommend all-three-pass, with the caveat that this rule was identified post-hoc and warrants independent replication.

items.title: MemoryForge introduces lifelong memory synthesis for LLM agents to enable human-like behaviors in role-play and user simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MemoryForge: Synthesize Lifelong Memory for Human-Like LLM Agents
items.summary:
MemoryForge is a new framework that equips large language models (LLMs) with human-like personas by synthesizing lifelong autobiographical memory from brief target personas. Unlike traditional methods that use static textual profiles, MemoryForge enables frozen LLMs to dynamically retrieve situation-relevant memories to guide their behavior, improving realism in agentic applications such as role-play and user simulation.

The framework includes a context generator for socio-historical grounding, a life organizer for developmental coherence, and a multi-resolution simulator balancing broad summaries with detailed episodic experiences. Experiments on PersonaGym and SimulatorArena demonstrate that MemoryForge's synthesized memory base helps frozen LLMs exhibit more human-like behaviors than strong descriptive conditioning baselines across multiple metrics and model backbones.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equipping Large Language Models (LLMs) with human-like personas is crucial for agentic applications, such as role-play and user simulation. Traditional prompt-based methods rely on descriptive conditioning by injecting static textual profiles, which often makes agents show generic behaviors due to a lack of realistic life memory. To fill this gap, we introduce memory-based conditioning, a paradigm inspired by the cognitive psychology, which replaces abstract profiles with an autobiographical memory base, enabling frozen LLMs to dynamically retrieve situation-relevant memory to guide their behaviors. We formalize its enabling task as customized lifelong memory synthesis and propose MemoryForge, a novel framework to synthesize such lifelong memory from brief target personas. MemoryForge has three key components: a context generator for socio-historical grounding, a life organizer for developmental coherence toward the target identity, and a multi-resolution simulator that balances broad temporal summaries with high-fidelity episodic experiences. Experiments on PersonaGym for role-play and SimulatorArena for user-simulation, show that the synthesized memory base by MemoryForge enables frozen LLMs to exhibit more human-like behaviors than strong descriptive conditioning baselines across multiple metrics and LLM backbones.

items.title: Researchers introduce Obshazard-bench to evaluate multimodal foundation models for real-time disaster intelligence using raw Earth observation data across 8 disaster categories in over 60 countries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Obshazard-bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Foundation Models for Real-Time Disaster Intelligence from Raw Earth Observation Streams
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Obshazard-bench, a real-time benchmark designed to assess multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in interpreting raw Earth observation data for disaster emergency response. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on static, expert-processed data, Obshazard-bench integrates high-frequency satellite streams with ground observations, historical disaster records, and socio-economic indicators to better reflect operational disaster scenarios.

The benchmark covers 8 major disaster categories and 28 sub-categories across more than 60 countries, including over 120 documented extreme events and thousands of visual question answering samples. It defines a three-stage evaluation aligned with disaster workflows: Predictive Crisis Anticipation, Active Evolution Reasoning, and Multi-faceted Impact Quantification. Experiments reveal significant challenges for current foundation models in converting raw multi-channel observations into timely and decision-relevant disaster insights.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret Earth observation data, yet their capability to support real-world disaster emergency response remains insufficiently evaluated. Existing remote sensing benchmarks largely rely on static, post-hoc, and expert-processed products, such as gridded reanalysis data, which are difficult to align with operational disaster scenarios where hazards evolve rapidly and decisions must be made under strict time constraints. To bridge this gap, we introduce Obshazard-bench, a real-time, observation-driven benchmark for evaluating disaster intelligence in MLLMs. Unlike image-centric or post-event benchmarks, Obshazard-bench directly integrates raw, high-frequency satellite sounding streams from diverse satellite sensors with concurrent ground-station observations, historical disaster records, and socio-economic indicators, bypassing delayed expert-processing and physical-inversion pipelines. The benchmark covers 8 major disaster categories and 28 sub-categories across more than 60 countries, incorporating over 120 historically documented extreme-event cases and thousands of lifecycle-oriented VQA samples. Moreover, Obshazard-bench further defines a three-stage evaluation taxonomy aligned with the operational disaster workflow: Predictive Crisis Anticipation for pre-disaster risk detection and early forecasting, Active Evolution Reasoning for in-situ disaster tracking and termination prediction, and Multi-faceted Impact Quantification for post-disaster magnitude deduction, humanitarian burden estimation, and socio-economic impact assessment. Experiments on representative general-purpose and Earth-focused foundation models reveal substantial limitations in transforming raw multi-channel physical observations into temporally grounded and decision-relevant disaster reasoning.

items.title: Researchers propose LLM-OSDA, a dynamic cost-per-click auction integrating optimal stopping for native ads in multi-turn LLM conversations, improving revenue by 11% over fixed-timing baselines [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM-OSDA: An Optimal-Stopping Dynamic Auction for Native Advertising in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
items.summary: LLM-OSDA is a new auction mechanism designed to embed native advertising within multi-turn large language model (LLM) conversations by dynamically determining the optimal timing to insert ads based on bids and contextual click quality. Unlike existing single-response ad auctions, LLM-OSDA couples timing and allocation decisions using Bellman optimal stopping and envelope pricing, ensuring truthful bidding is weakly dominant in expectation under an exact oracle. The system uses a learned StopNet to approximate optimal stopping decisions, with experiments on simulated conversational ad data showing an 11% net revenue increase compared to fixed-timing methods while maintaining similar user retention. This approach shifts the advertising unit from fixed slots to moments within evolving conversations, addressing challenges in timing and allocation coupling for LLM-native ads.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-native advertising embeds sponsored content directly into model-generated responses, shifting the unit of sale from a fixed slot to a moment within an evolving conversation. Existing LLM ad-auction mechanisms primarily operate within a single response, settling the winner but not the timing. The extension is nontrivial: with one native insertion opportunity per session, the stopping time depends on bids, coupling timing with allocation, so static truthfulness arguments no longer apply. We propose the LLM-based Optimal Stopping Dynamic Auction (LLM-OSDA), a dynamic cost-per-click auction that integrates Bellman optimal stopping, winner allocation, and envelope pricing. A bid-independent LLM layer estimates contextual click quality and seamlessly renders the winning ad, while bids enter only the committed auction mechanism. Under an exact Bellman oracle, the expected discounted-click allocation is monotone in each advertiser's bid, and the corresponding envelope payment makes truthful bidding weakly dominant in expectation. For practical deployment, a learned StopNet approximates the Bellman action values. We show that its decisions differ from the optimal policy only near the stopping boundary and bound the resulting incentive loss in terms of its approximation error. Experiments on a simulated conversational advertising corpus show that LLM-OSDA improves net revenue by 11 percent over the strongest fixed-timing baseline while maintaining comparable user retention. Code is at https://github.com/2025Fang2025/llm-osda.

items.title: Researchers introduce OSCD algorithm to improve native multilingual chain-of-thought reasoning in low-resource Southeast Asian languages, achieving up to 3.2 times better mathematical reasoning performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Native Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Low-Resource Southeast Asian Languages
items.summary: Large Language Models often revert to English during complex reasoning in low-resource native languages, limiting their effectiveness. Researchers propose the Onramp-Sequence Cross-Distillation (OSCD) algorithm, which projects high-resource reasoning paths into low-resource vocabularies and aligns semantic embeddings to bridge cross-lingual gaps. Evaluations on AIME25 and HMMT25 benchmarks show OSCD improves mathematical reasoning in Southeast Asian languages by up to 3.2 times, with semantic alignment contributing up to 6.4% improvement in reducing linguistic bias compared to translation-only methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models have achieved substantial progress in reasoning capabilities. Yet in low-resource native settings, many suffer from cross-lingual collapse, reverting to English during intermediate steps that require complex logical reasoning. This presents a cold-start bottleneck for policy optimization, whereas standard fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting due to cross-lingual representation drift. To address these challenges, we introduce the Onramp-Sequence Cross-Distillation (OSCD), a post-training algorithm that projects high-resource reasoning trajectories into low-resource vocabulary subspaces during generative training rollouts via an integrated translator agentic loop, ensuring the stable and efficient translation of dynamically generated reference samples for fine-tuning. This is coupled with joint-embedding semantic alignment of both reference and target-language reasoning traces, thereby bridging the pairwise cross-lingual representational gaps. Comprehensive evaluations using the AIME25 and HMMT25 benchmarks demonstrate that OSCD yields up to 3.2 times overall improvements in native Southeast Asian languages for mathematical reasoning, of which the joint-embedding semantic alignment component contributes up to 6.4% improvements in linguistic debiasing over translation-only baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose Test-Time Context Distillation to improve long-context language modeling by guiding models to retain information relevant for future predictions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning What to Remember: Test-Time Training via Context Distillation
items.summary: Researchers introduce Test-Time Context Distillation (TTCD), a framework that uses a long-window teacher to supervise a short-window student model, enabling better allocation of limited memory for future token prediction in long-context language tasks. The in-place variant, IP-TTCD, leverages existing model parameters for fast adaptation and outperforms prior methods like DeltaNet and sliding-window attention when trained from scratch. IP-TTCD also allows pre-trained transformers to adapt during inference with minimal architectural changes, advancing continual learning approaches for long-context capabilities.

The in-place variant, IP-TTCD, leverages existing model parameters for fast adaptation and outperforms prior methods like DeltaNet and sliding-window attention when trained from scratch. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.01672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective long-context modeling is not merely about retaining more of the past, but about preserving the information that may prove relevant later. Test-time training (TTT) is an appealing approach that performs online parameter updates for long-context modeling, yet existing TTT methods only optimize either reconstruction or online adaptation objectives without considering the future utility of retained information. In this work, we propose \textbf{T}est-\textbf{T}ime \textbf{C}ontext \textbf{D}istillation (TTCD), a TTT framework that introduces a self-supervised objective for allocating limited memory capacity for future use. Specifically, TTCD uses a long-window teacher to supervise the fast weights of a short-window student, where the hidden-state discrepancy between them offers a dense, self-supervised signal guiding the model to memorize the contextual information crucial for future token predictions. We focus on an in-place variant: In-Place TTCD (IP-TTCD), which uses the existing MLP parameters as the fast weights. Experiments on long-context language modeling tasks show IP-TTCD consistently outperforms DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, sliding-window attention, and TTT when pre-trained from scratch. Furthermore, IP-TTCD allows pre-trained transformer models to adapt their parameters during inference through continual pre-training, gaining long-context capabilities with only a lightweight architectural augmentation. Our results position TTCD as a step toward architectural continual learning.

items.originalTitle: Automatic Annotation of Ancient Greek Vowel Length
items.summary: Researchers have created the first general-purpose tool to automatically annotate vowel length in Ancient Greek texts, addressing the lack of large-scale macronized corpora. The system uses lemma, part-of-speech, and morphological data to infer vowel length, enabling less common word forms to inherit markings from more common ones. The macronizer also enhances downstream tasks such as verse scansion in prosodic natural language processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.01935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior work in Ancient Greek NLP relies on corpora that do not disambiguate the phonemic vowel length of alpha, iota, and ypsilon, together known as the dichrona. Depending on lexeme, morphology, sandhi, syntax, and conventions of period, genre, and verse form, each of these letters can represent either a long or a short vowel. Deciding and marking the correct length is known as "macronizing", a long-tail problem given the sheer mass of word forms and the context dependency of individual instances. No macronized corpus of Ancient Greek is publicly available at scale, so a stand-alone macronizer is needed. While previous work has shown how to build a static, corpus-bespoke vowel-length dictionary, the present paper constructs the first general-purpose macronizer for arbitrary Ancient Greek input. Given input carrying lemma, part-of-speech, and morphological annotation in the standard CoNLL-U format, a set of recursive modules lets less common word forms inherit markup from more common forms of the same lexical word. The macronizer's chief application is generating training data for machine learning: we show that a small character-level transformer trained on the macronizer's own output learns to generalize past the cases the rule-based system leaves unmarked, matching or exceeding its accuracy on a gold-standard, manually annotated benchmark of verse and prose. We also show that macronization can improve downstream prosodical NLP tasks like verse scansion.

items.title: Researchers define TextNCA, a hierarchical Neural Cellular Automata model with local attention for language modeling, analyzing its performance on WikiText-103 against Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TextNCA: Neural Cellular Automata for Language Modeling via Hierarchical Local Attention
items.summary:
Researchers introduce TextNCA, a 1D causal windowed-attention implementation of Neural Cellular Automata for language modeling, tested on WikiText-103 with about 30 million parameters. The hierarchical model uses three stages with varying window sizes and shared-weight iterations, but it does not outperform parameter-matched Transformers, serving instead as an analytical tool to understand the impact of local, iterated, and weight-shared computation primitives.

The study finds that the model's behavior is largely driven by a staged narrow-to-wide attention schedule, with iteration providing a smaller, bounded benefit optimized at four iterations. Components like the GRU gate and learned per-step embeddings are necessary for this benefit, and training with random iteration counts allows inference-time adjustment at the cost of higher perplexity. The work aims to clarify which aspects of Neural Cellular Automata computations contribute most to language modeling performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.02050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a strictly local, iterated, weight-shared computation primitive support language modelling, and which of those three properties actually drives the model's behaviour? We define \textsc{TextNCA}, a 1D causal windowed-attention realisation of the Neural Cellular Automaton primitive, and study a hierarchical variant that cascades three stages with windows $w \in \{8, 32, 128\}$ and $T_s$ shared-weight iterations per stage, all on WikiText-103 at roughly 30M parameters and 60k training steps. The model does not match a parameter-matched Transformer at this scale (Hier-TextNCA $60.3$ vs.\ Transformer-6L $52.8$ and Transformer-12L $44.7$ PPL), so we treat it as an analytical probe rather than a proposed alternative. The behaviour we observe is largely explained by the staged narrow-to-wide schedule: a non-iterating sliding-window Transformer that reuses the same schedule comes within $+4.1$ PPL of the iterated model, while reversing, flattening, or breaking the monotonic ordering of the schedule costs between $+16.7$ and $+70.8$ PPL. Iteration adds a smaller bounded benefit on top of the schedule, with a clear optimum at $T_s{=}4$ and a U-shaped degradation beyond it. The GRU gate and learned per-step embeddings are required for that benefit to appear, and training with random $T_s$ yields an inference-time iteration-count knob at the cost of substantially higher absolute PPL. We position the work as a controlled reading of which parts of NCA-style computation carry the weight in language modelling.

items.title: Researchers propose SPEE framework for self-improving large language models through progressive experience evolution and policy optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Improving Large Language Models via Progressive Experience Evolution
items.summary:
Researchers introduce SPEE (Self-Progressive Experience Evolution), a post-training framework designed to enable large language models (LLMs) to self-improve by transforming transient interaction experiences into persistent capabilities. SPEE combines explicit experience evolution, which extracts and refines knowledge from multiple interaction trajectories, with implicit policy optimization using reinforcement learning to explore new strategies. This approach addresses limitations in existing self-improvement methods that either extract experience without internalizing it or update model parameters without accumulating transferable experience.

SPEE maintains a global experience pool that consolidates knowledge from both successful and failed attempts, filters out low-utility experiences, and reduces biases from individual trajectories. Experiments on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that SPEE outperforms existing test-time and training-time self-evolution baselines across three model scales. The researchers have made the source code publicly available for further exploration and validation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.02139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) capable of self-improvement require not only effective policy optimization, but also a principled mechanism for transforming transient interaction experience into persistent model capabilities. Existing self-improvement paradigms remain fragmented: test-time methods can explicitly extract experience but cannot internalize it into model parameters, whereas training-time optimization methods can update model parameters but lack an explicit mechanism for accumulating transferable experience. Bridging these two paradigms requires a critical intermediate stage that remains underexplored, namely \emph{experience distillation}. To address this gap, we propose \textbf{SPEE} (\textbf{S}elf-\textbf{P}rogressive \textbf{E}xperience \textbf{E}volution), a unified post-training framework that sequentially performs explicit experience evolution followed by implicit policy optimization. During explicit experience evolution, SPEE reflects on trajectories collected from multiple interactions to extract, verify, and progressively evolve transferable experience, which is subsequently internalized into the policy through privilege-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). During implicit policy optimization, reward-driven reinforcement learning leverages these internalized priors to explore novel solution strategies. In the experience evolution stage, a continuously evolving global experience pool consolidates knowledge from both successful and failed trajectories, filters out low-utility experience, and mitigates post-hoc rationalization induced by individual trajectories. Experiments on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SPEE consistently outperforms both test-time and training-time self-evolution baselines across three model scales. The source code is available at https://github.com/rrrsj/SPEE.

items.title: TRACE-TS introduces attribution-grounded reasoning framework for wearable sensor data, improving human activity understanding with structured evidence and language model-generated reasoning traces [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TRACE-TS: Attribution-Grounded and Traceable Sensor-Language Reasoning for Human Activity Understanding
items.summary:
TRACE-TS is a new framework designed to enhance human activity recognition from wearable sensor data by generating structured, signal-grounded reasoning traces. It uses attribution from an expert classifier to identify key sensor regions and constructs directed acyclic graph (DAG) reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance, training a compact language model to generate these traces alongside activity predictions without needing attribution at inference.

The framework introduces Semantic Node Match (SNM), a metric that evaluates reasoning fidelity by detecting hallucinated observations and broken evidence chains missed by standard natural language generation metrics. Tested across seven wearable benchmarks, TRACE-TS achieved the highest average accuracy (84.43%) and F1 score (81.24%), outperforming the best large language model-based baseline by 17.96% in F1. The code for TRACE-TS is publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wearable sensors capture fine-grained motion patterns that support rich behavioral understanding, yet most existing methods reduce these signals to activity labels. Recent LM-based approaches generate natural-language explanations for sensor data, but their reasoning is weakly grounded in the underlying signal, leading to fluent yet unverifiable explanations. We introduce TRACE-TS (Traceable Reasoning with Attribution-Grounded Evidence), a framework for structured and signal-grounded reasoning over wearable time series. TRACE-TS uses attribution from an expert classifier to identify salient spatio-temporal sensor regions, uses them to construct DAG reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance, and trains a compact language model to generate these traces through gated cross-attention over sensor memory tokens. At inference, the adapted model jointly outputs the activity prediction and its reasoning trace, without requiring attribution computation or teacher guidance. We introduce Semantic Node Match(SNM), an LLM-as-judge metric that diagnoses reasoning fidelity at the observation, inference, and synthesis levels, localizing hallucinated observations and broken evidence chains missed by standard NLG metrics. Across seven wearable benchmarks, TRACE-TS achieves the best average accuracy and F1 among all evaluated methods (84.43%/81.24%), and outperforms the best LLM-based baseline by 17.96% in F1. Our code is available at https://github.com/SparshRastogi/TRACE-TS.

items.title: Researchers present RMSWeb, a three-part method improving web agent reinforcement learning for Qwen3-VL-Instruct models at 8B and 32B parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RMSWeb: Reflection, Failure-Mode Mining, and Salvage-DS for Web Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: RMSWeb addresses challenges in training compact web agents by introducing reflection-conditioned retries to increase data collection efficiency, failure-mode mining to focus offline reinforcement learning on critical states, and Salvage-DS to improve learning signals for rejected action groups. This approach reduces action steps by up to 19.7% on solved tasks and improves performance by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B on benchmarks including WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench. The 8B model achieves the strongest reported results among similarly sized open-weight models on Online-Mind2Web and demonstrates a leading accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench, noting differences in external evaluation protocols.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compact web agents can reduce deployment cost, but training them poses challenges in both data collection and post-SFT reinforcement learning (RL). Successful trajectories are expensive to collect and often contain inefficient detours. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), full trajectory corpora are dominated by routine states; moreover, when group-relative RL is applied to web actions, inadequately designed action-level rewards can yield weak or misleading relative updates, while groups rejected as unsuitable for such updates receive no fallback learning signal. We present RMSWeb, a three-part recipe for Qwen3-VL-Instruct at 8B and 32B. Reflection-conditioned retries increase collection yield and shorten successful trajectories; failure-mode mining concentrates offline RL on critical states exposed by the SFT policy; and Salvage-DS combines an action-semantic polarized reward, contrast-and-competence-gated dynamic sampling, and an action-only anchor for rejected groups. Policies trained with reflection-collected data use up to 19.7% fewer action steps on solved tasks. On WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench, RMSWeb improves over SFT by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B. Our 8B model also achieves the strongest reported Online-Mind2Web result among similarly sized open-weight models in our comparison and a leading reported accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench, with the caveat that external evaluation protocols differ.

items.title: Researchers present a unified LLMOps architecture integrating real-time data ingestion, continual learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and human feedback to improve large language model deployments in regulated sectors [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Unleashing the Potential of Large Language Models: A Blueprint for Real-Time, Enterprise-Ready Deployments
items.summary:
Researchers propose a pattern-driven LLMOps architecture that addresses challenges in real-time, regulated deployments of large language models, such as knowledge staleness, catastrophic forgetting, hallucination, and weak feedback loops. The architecture combines adaptive ingestion, continual learning, adaptive retrieval policies, and automated feedback-driven convergence into a single operational pipeline.

The approach includes four key components: an adaptive ingestion pattern orchestrator evaluated with FreshStreamBench; STAR+FAR continual learning with sparse temporal adapter routing and freshness-aware replay; SAGE, an SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy that predicts per-query passage budgets to meet tail-latency targets; and an automated feedback-driven convergence stage with reinforcement learning from human feedback triggers. This design aims to reduce latency, cost, and accuracy trade-offs while supporting auditability and rollback, making it suitable for high-risk sectors like health care and finance.

items.title: Researchers show chain-of-thought monitoring fails against adversaries who rewrite reasoning to hide exploits, dropping detection rates from 95% to under 11% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A False Average: Chain-of-Thought Monitors Collapse Where They Are the Only Defense
items.summary: Researchers demonstrate that chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring, designed to detect reward hacks that appear clean in actions but reveal themselves in reasoning, can be defeated by adversaries who rewrite only the reasoning while keeping commands and outputs unchanged. This approach drastically reduces a monitor's detection rate on targeted subsets, revealing that aggregate accuracy metrics mask near-total failures where CoT monitoring is the sole defense. The attack works across different monitor types and agent models, including live agents, and trace-only defenses recover only part of the evasion since the rewrite remains truthful about actions but falsifies intent. Additional analysis shows that some detection signals are due to detectors rather than genuine monitor understanding, indicating limitations in current CoT monitoring approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00583v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is meant to catch the reward hacks that look clean in the actions and betray themselves only in the reasoning. We show that this is exactly where an adversary who controls the reasoning can defeat it. Rewriting only an agent's reasoning to read as good-faith engineering, while copying every command and output verbatim so the exploit is unchanged, drops a held-out monitor's catch rate on that subset from about 95% to under 11% in one gradient-free shot. A monitor's aggregate accuracy is a false average: dominated by hacks the actions give away, it hides the near-total collapse this rewrite produces on the subset where CoT monitoring is the only signal. The attack transfers across monitor families and agent models, reproduces with live agents, though against a calibrated monitor evasion concentrates in the strongest agent. Trace-only defenses recover it only partially, even one primed on the attack, because the rewrite stays truthful about what happened and lies only about intent; only information from outside the trace helps substantially. A probe on an open-weight surrogate monitor's activations separates the hacks its verdict misses, but a causal control shows this is a detector, not evidence the monitor secretly knows.

items.title: Researchers develop a unified framework for dense language generation algorithms achieving optimal lower-density guarantees with deterministic and randomized methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dense Language Generation Made Simple: Deterministic, Randomized, and Multi-Order Algorithms
items.summary:
Researchers present a theoretical framework for language generation that ensures generators produce new valid strings from a stream of examples while maintaining validity and novelty. They introduce a simple deterministic algorithm achieving the optimal lower-density guarantee of 1/2 and extend it with randomized algorithms that improve this guarantee to 1-1/e against oblivious adversaries. Their framework also supports multiple orders of output importance simultaneously without loss in performance.

The work builds on prior measures of output coverage called lower density, which quantifies the fraction of important outputs generated before appearing in the data. The researchers provide a simpler analysis than previous studies and demonstrate the flexibility of their approach through extensions that accommodate randomization and multiple relevance orders. This contributes to understanding how language generators can reliably and efficiently cover diverse outputs in adversarial settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.01320v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language generation in the limit is a theoretical framework for studying how a generator can learn to produce new valid strings from a stream of positive examples. In this model, an adversary chooses an unknown language from a countable family and enumerates its elements in an arbitrary order, while the generator must eventually output only elements of the language that have not yet appeared in the enumeration. Reliable generation is thus formalized through two eventual guarantees: validity and novelty relative to the observed data. To further quantify the breadth of the generator's outputs, Kleinberg and Wei (FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) introduced lower density as a measure of output coverage. Given an order representing the importance or relevance of possible outputs, lower density is the asymptotic lower bound, as $n$ grows, on the fraction of the first $n$ elements of the target language that the generator outputs before they appear in the data. Kleinberg and Wei showed that $1/2$ is the optimal lower-density guarantee for deterministic algorithms. We develop a simple and unified framework for obtaining optimal lower-density guarantees. We first give a deterministic algorithm that recovers the optimal guarantee of $1/2$ with a significantly simpler analysis than prior work. We then demonstrate the flexibility of our framework through two extensions. First, against an oblivious adversary, randomization raises the optimal guarantee to $1-1/e$. Second, for any finite collection of orders, the optimal deterministic and randomized guarantees can be achieved simultaneously with respect to every order, so accommodating multiple notions of importance or relevance entails no loss in the optimal guarantee.

items.title: Researchers develop self-evolving curriculum using Question-begets-Question method to improve reinforcement fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-Math-7B on competition math problems, raising pass@1 accuracy from 5.6% to 16.5% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Question Begets Question: Self-Evolving Curriculum for Reinforcement Fine-Tuning on Competition Mathematics
items.summary:
Researchers addressed challenges in teaching a language model competition mathematics by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-7B, which initially solved only 5.6% of problems. They introduced Question-begets-Question (QbQ), a method that generates diverse problem variants to overcome data scarcity and trained the model using reinforcement learning without relying on ground-truth reasoning traces. Static training with augmented data plateaued at 14.5% accuracy, but a self-evolving curriculum that iteratively retrains on variants of problems the model mostly solves broke this ceiling, reaching 16.5% pass@1 accuracy after 20 rounds with no saturation.

The approach counterintuitively showed that training on problems the model can mostly solve leads to improvements and enables the model to tackle harder, unseen problems. This method demonstrates a scalable way to enhance language model performance on complex reasoning tasks despite limited data and absent oracle reasoning traces.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.01522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Teaching a language model a skill it has not mastered is obstructed by three recurring difficulties: training data is scarce, ground-truth reasoning traces are usually unavailable, and models often exhibit an apparent ceiling beyond which additional data yields no further improvement. We study these difficulties in a controlled setting, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-7B on competition mathematics (AIME), a task on which it initially solves only 5.6\% of problems (pass@1). To address data scarcity, we introduce Question-begets-Question (QbQ), a scalable procedure in which a teacher transforms existing problems into diverse variants that probe the same underlying skills; to model the absence of oracle reasoning, we train exclusively via reinforcement learning on problem statements and final answers, never on teacher reasoning traces. Static training on such data, however, plateaus well short of the task: real-plus-synthetic augmentation and non-curriculum QbQ generated synthetic data training cap pass@1 at 12.5\% and 14.5\% respectively, despite large increases in data. Our central finding is that this ceiling is not intrinsic to the model. We propose a self-evolving curriculum that, each round, evaluates the current checkpoint, seeds QbQ from the problems it can mostly get right, and trains on the resulting variants; under an identical data budget, this breaks the ceiling and lifts pass@1 to 16.5\% with no sign of saturation after 20 rounds. Counterintuitively, we find that models improve when trained on variants of problems they can mostly get right, and that models trained this way go on to solve harder problems never seen during training.

items.title: Study finds no reliable benefit from competitive adversarial self-play in legal reasoning models across multiple tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Does the Competitive Component of Adversarial Self-Play Improve Legal Reasoning? A Controlled Negative Result
items.summary: Researchers tested whether the competitive component of adversarial self-play—where a student model drafts legal arguments and an adversary attacks them, with rewards for surviving attacks—improves legal reasoning. Using a verifiable survival reward system that checks citations, they compared competitive training to non-competitive training across four independent evaluations and a pilot with a stronger adversary, finding no significant advantage for the competitive approach. Early apparent benefits were attributed to small-sample artifacts, and metrics used revealed pitfalls such as collapsing to recall when adversaries ceased citing gold-standard authorities. This negative result aligns with prior findings in coding domains that the value of multi-teacher curricula lies in verifiable environments rather than competition itself.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.01559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial self-play is an appealing recipe for legal reasoning: have a student model draft an argument, have an adversary attack it, and reward the student when its argument survives the attack. We designed exactly such a training signal -- a verifiable "survival" reward in which both the student's cited authorities and the adversary's counter-authorities are checked by a citation verifier, so that survival is decided on verified grounds rather than rhetoric, and fabricated citations are automatically neutralized. We then asked a narrow but important question: does the competitive component itself -- the adversary and the survival reward -- add anything on top of an otherwise identical non-competitive training run? Across four independent tests -- a bootstrap comparison, a two-seed replication, a paired per-case adversarial-robustness comparison, and a blinded head-to-head judgment of generated arguments, plus a follow-up pilot with a deliberately strengthened self-play adversary -- the competitive component produced no reliable benefit. The blinded judgment gave a 49% win rate (binomial p approx. 1.000); the strengthened-adversary pilot gave a 50% win rate (32:32, p approx. 1.000). An early apparent +29% advantage reversed and proved to be a small-sample artifact. We report this as an honest negative result. The value of the paper is reproducibility and the sharing of concrete pitfalls: an initially promising metric that inverted on more data, and an adversarial-robustness metric that silently collapsed to plain recall once the adversary stopped citing the same authorities as the gold answer. This null is consistent with, and reconfirms in the legal domain, the conclusion of the companion coding-domain study (Kim, 2026, arXiv:2607.08255) that the value of multi-teacher curricula arises from constructing a verifiable environment rather than from competition itself.

items.title: Researchers introduce LongCat Sparse Attention, a hardware-algorithm co-designed framework that reduces indexing overhead and memory inefficiency for long-context AI models up to one million tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LongCat Sparse Attention: Taming the Lightning via Streaming-aware Hierarchical Cross-Layer Indexing
items.summary: LongCat Sparse Attention (LSA) addresses system-level bottlenecks in DeepSeek Sparse Attention by combining streaming-aware indexing, cross-layer indexing, and hierarchical indexing to improve hardware efficiency and reduce computation. The framework achieves performance comparable to full attention across models ranging from 69 billion to 560 billion parameters and supports native training with extremely long context lengths. LSA underpins the development of LongCat-2.0 and is integrated into the open-source LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse model, which includes an updated long-context training corpus to facilitate further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.01662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) enables efficient long-context modeling through its Lightning Indexer. However, practical deployment remains constrained by the indexer's expensive $O(L^2)$ scoring overhead and the hardware-inefficient, discontinuous memory-access patterns induced by its outputs. To address these system-level bottlenecks, we introduce LongCat Sparse Attention (LSA), a hardware-algorithm co-designed framework comprising three complementary and orthogonal strategies: (1) Streaming-Aware Indexing, which selectively converts scattered KV entries into hardware-aligned contiguous layouts to enable coalesced HBM access; (2) Cross-Layer Indexing, which amortizes indexing overhead by reusing the results produced by a single layer across consecutive layers, supported by cross-layer distillation; and (3) Hierarchical Indexing, which adopts a coarse-to-fine scoring scheme to progressively narrow the candidate set for each query, thereby substantially reducing indexing computation. Extensive scaling experiments, ranging from 69B-A3B to 560B-A27B models, demonstrate that LSA consistently achieves performance on par with full attention across both general-purpose and long-context benchmarks. Moreover, LSA supports native training with context lengths of up to one million tokens and underpins the development of LongCat-2.0 (1.6T-A48B). To facilitate further research, we also introduce and open-source LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse (69B-A3B), which integrates LSA into LongCat-Flash-Lite and incorporates an updated long-context training corpus.

items.title: Researchers propose geometry-guided layerwise feed-forward network width allocation in Transformers, improving validation loss over uniform and cosine taper schedules [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Geometry-Guided Layerwise FFN Width Allocation in Transformers
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a method to allocate feed-forward network (FFN) widths in Transformer models based on geometric changes measured during forward passes, rather than using constant widths across layers. They quantify these changes using metrics like correspondence-preserving shift, Gromov-Wasserstein distortion, and persistent homology, and develop an exact fixed-budget optimizer for layerwise width allocation.

Testing across seven pretrained language models and training runs with 128M, 256M, and 440M parameters, the geometry-based allocation schedules, especially those using normalized work metrics, consistently reduce mean validation loss compared to uniform width and hand-designed cosine taper schedules. The study finds that raw Euclidean work correlates with residual-norm growth, while Gromov-Wasserstein work aligns better with layer sensitivity, suggesting geometry-informed width allocation can enhance Transformer training efficiency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.02064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) account for a large fraction of Transformer parameters, yet their hidden width is usually constant across depth. We ask whether this capacity can instead be allocated from a forward-pass measurement of layer behavior. We view each FFN as transporting a cloud of token representations and quantify the induced geometric change using correspondence-preserving shift, Gromov-Wasserstein distortion, and degree-one persistent homology under raw and scale-normalized metrics. A layerwise approximation surrogate yields an exact fixed-budget optimizer. Across seven pretrained language models, raw Euclidean work largely tracks residual-norm growth, whereas normalized work is predominantly front-loaded. Gromov-Wasserstein work is more consistently associated with perturbation-based layer sensitivity than the finite-sample topological estimate. In paired 128M and 256M training runs, several normalized-work schedules reduce mean validation loss relative to both uniform width and a hand-designed cosine taper. With the amplified paired differences at 440M, the best geometry-based allocations improve over uniform substantially larger than the cosine taper, while the anti-topological raw control is worse than uniform.

items.title: Researchers propose Instruction-Conditioned Exploration with Asymmetric Reinforcement Learning and Self-Distillation to improve large language model training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Instruction-Conditioned Exploration with Asymmetric Reinforcement Learning and Self-Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Instruction-Conditioned Exploration (ICE), a method that supplements task prompts with distinct instructions during training to increase behavioral diversity in large language models (LLMs). They combine this with an Asymmetric Reinforcement Learning and Self-Distillation (Asymmetric-RL/SD) objective to transfer learned behaviors to the unconditioned test-time policy, enhancing model performance.

Applying ICE with the Asymmetric-RL/SD objective to the Qwen3-1.7B model improves pass@1 accuracy on mathematical reasoning tasks by 5.0% at a 4,000-token response length compared to training with DAPO, with gains persisting at an 8,000-token context length. This approach addresses challenges in exploration due to the LLM action-space structure and leverages pre-trained model flexibility to generate diverse training experiences.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.02087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important tool for improving model capabilities, but the LLM action-space structure introduces challenges distinct from classical RL, with implications for inducing exploration. New methods are required that leverage the broad knowledge and flexibility of pre-trained LLMs to deliberately generate diverse experience at training time. We propose Instruction-Conditioned Exploration (ICE), which supplements task prompts during training with one of several distinct instructions, increasing the coverage of behaviours attempted. To facilitate ICE, we propose Asymmetric-RL/SD, a combined Reinforcement Learning and Self-Distillation training objective, to transfer explored behaviours to the unconditioned test-time policy. ICE with the Asymmetric-RL/SD objective improves Qwen3-1.7B held-out pass@1 performance at $4$K response length on mathematical reasoning tasks by $5.0\%$ relative to training with DAPO, with improvement persisting at a longer 8K context.

items.originalTitle: Computational Approaches to Understanding Large Language Model Impact on Writing and Information Ecosystems
items.summary: This dissertation explores how large language models (LLMs) are transforming writing and communication by analyzing institutional adoption, usage patterns, and feedback capabilities. It identifies systematic biases introduced by AI detectors that disadvantage writers using non-dominant language varieties, raising equity concerns in AI governance. The study also presents algorithmic methods to measure LLM adoption across various writing domains, including academic peer reviews, scientific publications, and corporate communications. Additionally, it evaluates LLMs' potential to provide manuscript feedback, particularly benefiting early-career and under-resourced researchers who face challenges in accessing timely reviews.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2506.17467v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant potential to change how we write, communicate, and create, leading to rapid adoption across society. This dissertation examines how individuals and institutions are adapting to and engaging with this emerging technology through three research directions. First, I demonstrate how the institutional adoption of AI detectors introduces systematic biases, particularly disadvantaging writers of non-dominant language varieties, highlighting critical equity concerns in AI governance. Second, I present novel population-level algorithmic approaches that measure the increasing adoption of LLMs across writing domains, revealing consistent patterns of AI-assisted content in academic peer reviews, scientific publications, consumer complaints, corporate communications, job postings, and international organization press releases. Finally, I investigate LLMs' capability to provide feedback on research manuscripts through a large-scale empirical analysis, offering insights into their potential to support researchers who face barriers in accessing timely manuscript feedback, particularly early-career researchers and those from under-resourced settings.

items.title: Researchers introduce Self-Correction Bench to reveal a 64.5% self-correction blind spot in large language models, showing models correct external but not internal errors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers developed Self-Correction Bench, a framework that distinguishes whether large language models (LLMs) fail to correct errors due to inability or lack of activation. Testing 14 open-source models revealed a 64.5% blind spot where models corrected externally attributed errors but failed on identical internal errors, indicating the capability exists but is not triggered. The study traced this issue to the absence of error-correction sequences in fine-tuning data and showed that fine-tuning with just over 5,000 such sequences reduced the blind spot by 76%. Additionally, appending the word "Wait" to prompts reduced the blind spot by 89.3% without additional training, suggesting multiple mechanisms govern self-correction activation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2507.02778v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have transformed AI, they still make errors and follow unproductive reasoning paths. Self-correction is vital for safety-critical applications, but studying it requires disentangling activation failure from knowledge deficiency: when a model fails to correct an error, is it because it cannot, or because it does not? We introduce Self-Correction Bench, a controlled evaluation framework that isolates this distinction by injecting the same error as either an external (user-attributed) or internal (model-attributed) error, keeping all other context identical. Testing 14 open-source non-reasoning models reveals a 64.5% Self-Correction Blind Spot: models correct external errors but fail on identical internal ones, proving the capability exists but is not activated. On models' own naturally generated errors, a measurable share of what a model fails to catch in its own output is caught when the identical error is presented externally. We trace the cause to post-training data composition: supervised fine-tuning datasets lack error-correction sequences, and fine-tuning with as few as 5,306 such traces already reduces the blind spot by 76.0%. Mechanistically, we identify a transferable conversational-role direction in representation space that causally gates self-correction. Appending "Wait" requires no training yet reduces the blind spot by 89.3%, and operates through a nearly independent pathway, indicating that correction activation is not reducible to this single mechanism.

items.originalTitle: Interpretable Recognition of Cognitive Distortions in Natural Language Texts
items.summary: Researchers have developed a new approach for multi-factor classification of natural language texts that uses weighted structured patterns like N-grams and accounts for heterarchical relationships between them. This method aims to automate the detection of specific cognitive distortions relevant to psychological care through an interpretable, robust, and transparent AI model. The proposed recognition and learning algorithms demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods, as tested on two publicly available datasets with optimized hyper-parameters. The team has made the code and models available for community use.

items.originalTitle: Visualising Information Flow in Word Embeddings with Diffusion Tensor Imaging
items.summary: Researchers present a novel method using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to analyze and visualize how information flows in natural language expressions within large language models (LLMs). This approach tracks changes in embedding space representations between tokens, offering insights beyond traditional single-word embedding visualizations and improving model interpretability. The method enables comparison of different LLM structures and may help identify under-utilized layers for potential pruning. Their findings suggest that DTI-based visualization provides a deeper understanding of how LLMs represent natural language in context.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.05713v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) represent natural language is a central challenge in natural language processing (NLP) research. Many existing methods extract word embeddings from an LLM, visualise the embedding space via point-plots, and compare the relative positions of certain words. However, this approach only considers single words and not whole natural language expressions, thus disregards the context in which a word is used. Here we present a novel tool for analysing and visualising information flow in natural language expressions by applying diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to word embeddings. We find that DTI reveals how embedding space representations change between tokens. Tracking these changes within the layers of an LLM allows for comparing different model structures and could potentially reveal opportunities for pruning an LLM's under-utilised layers. Our results show that our visualisation method permits novel insights into how LLMs represent actual natural language expressions, extending the comparison of isolated word embeddings and improving the interpretability of NLP models.

items.title: MAPLE introduces metadata-augmented in-context learning to improve differentially private synthetic data generation for domain-specific language models, reducing API costs and improving convergence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MAPLE: Metadata Augmented Private Language Evolution
items.summary:
MAPLE addresses the challenge of differentially private fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) when direct model access is unavailable by generating synthetic data grounded in private tabular metadata. This method enhances Private Evolution (PE) by using metadata to better initialize synthetic data distributions, improving alignment with specialized domain data and overcoming convergence and utility issues common in prior approaches.

Evaluations on domain-specific text generation tasks demonstrate that MAPLE achieves a superior privacy-utility trade-off, converges faster, and significantly lowers API usage costs compared to baseline PE methods. This approach enables practical, privacy-preserving adaptation of LLMs via API-based frameworks without requiring full model access or extensive compute resources.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.19258v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Differentially private (DP) fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) requires massive compute and full model access, which rules out state-of-the-art proprietary APIs for general users. Generating DP synthetic data offers a practical workaround. This approach also allows for transparent exploratory data analysis and arbitrary reuse across downstream tasks, sidestepping the rigid constraints of a model's parameter space. Private Evolution (PE) provides a promising API-based framework for generating this data, but its success relies heavily on initialization. If the private data distribution falls too far outside the foundation model's pre-training priors -- a common issue in highly specialized domain -- PE struggles to align with the target data. This misalignment causes poor convergence, degraded utility, and wasted API calls. To solve this initialization bottleneck, we introduce Metadata Augmented Private Language Evolution (MAPLE). MAPLE extracts DP tabular metadata and uses in-context learning to firmly ground the initial synthetic distribution in the target domain. Our evaluations on domain-specific text generation tasks show that MAPLE yields a strictly better privacy-utility trade-off, converges significantly faster, and sharply reduces API costs compared to baseline PE methods.

items.title: LangFIR identifies sparse language-specific features from monolingual data to improve language steering in multilingual large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LangFIR: Discovering Sparse Language-Specific Features from Monolingual Data for Language Steering
items.summary: LangFIR is a method that discovers sparse, language-specific features in large language models using only small amounts of monolingual data and random-token sequences, enabling more reliable control of output language. It filters out language-agnostic features to isolate those that are highly selective and causally important for specific languages, improving multilingual generation accuracy across multiple models, datasets, and languages. The approach outperforms previous methods relying on parallel data, suggesting that language identity in multilingual models is localized in sparse feature directions discoverable without expensive multilingual resources.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.03532v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show strong multilingual capabilities, yet reliably controlling the language of their outputs remains difficult. Representation-level steering addresses this by adding language-specific vectors to model activations at inference time, but identifying language-specific directions in the residual stream often relies on multilingual or parallel data that can be expensive to obtain. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose residual activations into interpretable, sparse feature directions and offer a natural basis for this search, yet existing SAE-based approaches face the same data constraint. We introduce LangFIR (Language Feature Identification via Random-token Filtering), a method that discovers language-specific SAE features using only a small amount of monolingual data and random-token sequences. Many SAE features consistently activated by target-language inputs do not encode language identity. Random-token sequences surface these language-agnostic features, allowing LangFIR to filter them out and isolate a sparse set of language-specific features. We show that these features are extremely sparse, highly selective for their target language, and causally important: directional ablation increases cross-entropy loss only for the corresponding language. Using these features to construct steering vectors for the multilingual generation control task, LangFIR achieves the best average accuracy x BLEU among steering methods across three models (Gemma 3 1B, Gemma 3 4B, and Llama 3.1 8B), three datasets, and twelve target languages, outperforming the strongest monolingual baseline by up to 4.7x and surpassing methods that use parallel data. Our results suggest that language identity in multilingual LLMs is localized in a sparse set of feature directions discoverable with monolingual data. Code is available at https://github.com/JaMussCraft/LangFIR

items.title: Researchers introduce Tensor Mixture (MixT), a Hamiltonian-inspired local-operator ansatz to reduce parameters and computation in large language models like Qwen3-8B and LLaMA2-7B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Hamiltonian-Inspired Local-Operator Ansatz for Slimming Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers propose Tensor Mixture (MixT), a method inspired by quantum many-body physics that represents dense neural network maps as sums of overlapping local tensor operators, aiming to reduce parameter and computational burdens in large language models. They tested MixT on Qwen3-8B and LLaMA2-7B models, finding a broad regime where accuracy is maintained before a sharp, model-specific boundary where performance changes abruptly. This approach also reduces arithmetic, storage, and memory requirements while revealing structural properties of learned linear maps at billion-parameter scale.
